$comment: Source of truth for which tests back each capability claim in PARITY_MATRIX.md.
scripts/check-parity.mjs verifies that every cited file exists and that the
matrix's yes/— columns match these citations exactly. An earlier revision of
the matrix claimed integration coverage for three capabilities that had none;
this file makes that class of claim checkable rather than a matter of trust.
Cite a file only when it genuinely exercises the capability.
A capability may also carry a `clauses` inventory: one entry per specification
clause, each with the real section reference and evidence naming a *test*
rather than a file. scripts/lib/clause-gate.mjs refuses a PASS whose mandatory
clauses are not evidenced. PARITY_MATRIX.md, under 'Clause-level evidence',
explains the six statuses and which of them block a PASS. Do not widen an
existing citation to cover a clause it does not test: that is the exact move
the gate exists to catch, and tests/unit/clause-gate.test.ts proves it does.

clauses.requirement: Notify when a provider disconnects.
clauses.note: Closed in Wave 16. The clause had no producer: an account only ever became `disconnected` during cloud-metadata restore, a backend path, and a rejected credential surfaced as a task error. There are now two producers, both in the worker's task lifecycle layer and neither in any adapter. At resolve time — which runs at the start of every task, resume and scheduled run — a provider that rejects its stored credentials marks the account `disconnected` and notifies. Mid-run, a credential revoked during a task reaches the lifecycle observer as a terminal AUTH_EXPIRED, which the provider layer treats as terminal because a rejected key is rejected on every retry; a rate limit or a 503 is deliberately not treated as a disconnect. The notification carries the build's own provider id and never the account's display name, endpoint or key.

clauses.requirement: allowedTools
clauses.note: Not implemented, and the reason is the architecture rather than effort. A shortcut here is an **alias, not an execution path**: there is no `shortcut.run`, and invoking one is two steps the panel takes — resolve the name, show the user what it means, then call workflow.replay or skill.run. So a shortcut carries no execution authority to narrow. The tool set is bounded where it is actually determined: a skill's reachable tools are derived from its steps at registration, composition included, and a workflow's are fixed by its recording. Putting a second allow-list on the name would add an authorization input to an object that does not execute, which is the second authorization surface this architecture refuses. Recorded as a divergence rather than a gap, and left mandatory so the matrix cannot read as fully satisfying §50.

clauses.requirement: permissionProfile
clauses.note: Not implemented, deliberately, and this one is a security position rather than a scoping one. A named permission profile attached to a shortcut is a **stored permission with a name on it**. The workflow and shortcut design turns on the opposite rule: a recording never becomes a standing grant, and replay re-earns every approval it needs at the risk the action actually carries. A profile would make the easiest path through the product the one that pre-approves. Recorded as a divergence, and left mandatory for the same reason as C5.

clauses.requirement: Check context capacity.
clauses.note: Closed in Wave 17, and precise about what it establishes. §14 lists nine minimum checks; eight were performed and the ninth was absent from the report entirely, while the context window was copied from the advertised model table. There is now a real probe: the model must carry a substantial prompt and the provider must report its own token count for it. That is a measured **floor**, not the window, and the check's own text says so — the window is still reported as this build's advertised figure and is labelled as not measured. Finding the ceiling would mean billing the user for a diagnostic, and reading it from provider model metadata is not uniformly available. The floor catches what the table cannot: an account tier whose usable context is far below the number published for the model.
